articles.title: There is only one Global South phrase for the APEC agenda: debt relief
articles.author: Vijay Prashad
articles.content: In October, I visited a steel factory in Xinyu, Jiangxi province. There was no dust in the factory. At a desk, a woman wearing an orange hard hat monitored the production of silicon-steel strips. Her attention moved between the machinery and her keyboard. “Keep the belt at the proper speed,” she said. The precision of the process depended on her knowledge as much as on the equipment before her. Here was innovation at work, sustained by the skills of a worker. That scene stayed with me as I considered the forthcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. A factory requires more than a machine purchased on the world market, it requires reliable electricity, transportation, technical education, and the accumulated capabilities of an industrial workforce. These foundations take years to build. They depend on sustained investment and on public institutions able to plan beyond the immediate horizon. For countries across the Global South, building this capacity is the substance of development. The leaders gathering in Shenzhen should ask whether the international financial system allows poorer countries to make such investments. How can they train workers and build modern industries when interest payments consume the resources required for schools, energy and infrastructure? Discussions about trade and technology must confront the conditions under which production becomes possible. The promise of shared prosperity will remain unfulfilled unless APEC addresses the destruction produced by war and the suffocation produced by debt. The major countries of the Global South – from Africa, Latin America, and South Asia – are, of course, missing from the APEC participants. But amongst those who will be at the table to represent the Global South are China, Indonesia, Mexico, Papua New Guinea, Peru, and Vietnam. They bring different histories and economic structures to the table, yet they have a shared interest in preserving the capacity of our countries to develop, to strengthen public services, and to cooperate across political differences. Cooperation succeeds when it expands possibilities beyond the region of the Asia-Pacific. The theme of APEC (Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together) establishes an important ambition for innovation and cooperation. At Shenzhen, the main agenda ideas will be for paperless trade and building cooperation for digital systems to reduce the cost for business as well as toward a Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific. These are worthwhile objectives, particularly when fragmentation of the world economy threatens the productive relationships built across the Pacific. The poorer nations at the table – Indonesia, Papua New Guinea, and the Philippines – will know that talk of digital infrastructure needs public investment, reliable energy, trained workers, and public institutions capable of directing technological change towards social needs. An agenda for connectivity must confront the financial conditions that prevent our societies from connecting on equitable terms. That means insisting on a serious discussion of debt. UN Trade and Development’s latest report , “A World of Debt 2026: Rising Debt Costs and Stalling Development,” describes a financial system increasingly hostile to development. Developing countries’ public debt reached $35 trillion in 2025. Their net interest payments reached $995 billion. In 51 developing countries, home to 3.7 billion people, governments spent more on interest than on either health or education. The injustice becomes clearer when the cost of borrowing is examined. UNCTAD reports average interest rates on public debt of 5.2% for developing countries, compared with 2.2% for developed economies. It estimates that borrowing at comparable rates could save developing countries around $500 billion annually. UNCTAD’s separate 2026 report on external debt sustainability reinforces the warning. Developing countries’ external debt reached $12.3 trillion in 2025, while interest costs on long-term external debt increased by almost 14%. Least developed countries devoted 18.2% of their export earnings to external debt service. Borrowing becomes a treadmill when the income earned through production is continually absorbed by obligations inherited from earlier years. Development plans remain on paper while payments leave the treasury. When interest costs overwhelm public resources because of unequal borrowing terms, the borrowing loses its developmental purposes. Without substantial debt relief for countries whose obligations have become unsustainable, there will be no possibility of the broad advance that the Global South requires. APEC cannot cancel sovereign debt by declaration, but it can raise the issue as a fundamental barrier for its main objectives – such as the importance of a digital landscape. APEC can build political support for action on debt relief and cancellation through the United Nations, the G20, and the development banks (the APEC Finance Ministers’ Process works with the Asian Development Bank, the Inter-American Development Bank, and the World Bank, but it also has project funds to support capacity building and technical cooperation). A credible agenda would begin with timely restructuring and meaningful reductions in unsustainable debt burdens. It would be very useful for APEC to join the debate around debt settlement that helps restore the capacity of poorer countries to develop, with their population’s welfare central to the calculation. In the October 2026, APEC finance ministers’ meeting, they affirmed that financial services should be accessible and affordable, particularly for individuals, households, and small businesses. This commitment to financial inclusion should be extended to the poorer nations, who cannot raise affordable funding for development. The APEC digital infrastructure statement from that meeting talked about the need for multilateral development banks to “ensure that scarce concessional and public resources catalyze, rather than replace, private investment.” But this is not enough. We need to be in discussion about debt settlement and about new finance that is not unfairly expensive. There needs to be an APEC-wide entitlement to concessional development loans or a debt-cancellation mechanism (at least one APEC state, Papua New Guinea is at high risk of debt distress, while two of them, Indonesia and the Philippines, sustain high debt by domestic borrowing with high rates of interest payments as part of their government finances). China can use its convening role to connect these issues. Shenzhen’s productive achievements provide an appropriate setting to discuss the foundations of development: infrastructure, education, industrial capacity, and sustained investment. The most valuable contribution of the summit would be to widen access to those foundations. Cooperation on technology should strengthen productive capabilities across developing economies, supported by financing arrangements that allow them to retain the gains of their own labor. The summit should be judged by whether its commitments enlarge the space for development. A declaration on innovation will mean little to a government forced to cut its education budget. A promise of connectivity will remain distant where interest payments absorb investment funds. The Global South should arrive in Shenzhen with a clear proposition: prosperity requires the resources to build it. That is an agenda worthy of the Pacific and its peoples. Vijay Prashad is an Indian historian and journalist. He is the author of forty books, including Washington Bullets, Red Star Over the Third World, The Darker Nations: A People’s History of the Third World, The Poorer Nations: A Possible History of the Global South, and How the International Monetary Fund Suffocates Africa, written with Grieve Chelwa. He is the executive director of Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research , the chief correspondent for Globetrotter, and an editor at LeftWord Books (New Delhi). He also appeared in the films Shadow World (2016) and Two Meetings (2017). This article was produced by Globetrotter .

articles.title: ASEAN summit in Manila met with protests over Trump’s participation
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: The 49th summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) opened in Manila, the Philippines on Sunday, November 15, amid large-scale protests against the presence of US President Donald Trump. Security forces clashed with protesters, injuring several and detaining hundreds, as they tried to march towards the Philippines International Convention Center. The protesters, carrying posters and banners with slogans against the US and Trump, the illegal war against Iran, and the proposed Pax Silica project in the country, tried to march to the venue of the summit despite police calling the protests illegal and erecting barricades to stop them. The Pax Silica is a global project proposed and led by the US. It is envisaged as a global supply chain for AI and chip making. The Philippines is one among 26 signatories of the proposed project launched in December last year with an objective to counter Chinese prominence in the industry. The environmental and human rights groups in the Philippines have opposed the project as it is expected to cause a negative impact on the environment and may cause the massive displacement of people from their ancestral land. Student groups, progressive parties, and trade unions also held Trump responsible for the war on Iran which has caused massive shortages of energy and a surge in the price of essential commodities. South China Sea code of conduct The summit began with Philippines President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Junior calling for greater regional unity. On Monday, several regional and global leaders are expected to address the summit. ASEAN has 11 members: Indonesia, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Thailand, Brunei, Singapore, and Timor Leste. The body was established in 1967 and it has a cumulative population of over 700 million. Apart from the 10 heads of member states (Myanmar remains suspended due to military take over in 2021 and its suppression of political dissent), US President Donald Trump, Chinese Premier Li Qiang, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, among others, are also participating. During his inaugural address, Marcos Junior also highlighted the need for progress towards the South China Sea Code of Conduct, which he has claimed he wanted to achieve during his country’s ASEAN presidency. The Code of Conduct (COC) aims to resolve the occasional disputes between some of the ASEAN countries and China in the South China Sea due to overlapping claims of sovereignty. However, it has remained incomplete for years and missed several deadlines. Addressing the summit on Monday, Chinese Premier Li Qiang also said that his country is looking forward to the early conclusion of the COC as it will “provide a solid institutional guarantee for lasting peace and stability” in the region, Xinhua reported . US-Israeli war on Iran Marcos Junior also pointed out the major areas of concern for the grouping, including the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has caused an unprecedented shortage of oil and energy products in the region. Because of the war on Iran and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, most of the countries in ASEAN who depend heavily on imports from the Middle East, particularly the Philippines and Malaysia, faced massive shortages of oil and other energy supplies, which led to increases in the prices of other essential commodities. The Philippines adopted emergency measures in March in response to energy shortages. The ASEAN summit in May called for an immediate end of the war and opening of the Strait of Hormuz. On Sunday, protesters from the New Patriotic Alliance claimed that Trump was responsible for the shortages and the economic hardships the citizens of the Philippines and other countries in the region have been facing for the last few months. They demanded that he should not be allowed to participate in the summit. The government of the Philippines has deployed thousands of security personnel around the venue of the summit as several groups have called for similar protests in the coming days.

articles.title: The fall of the ANC
articles.author: Pavan Kulkarni
articles.content: Securing less than 31% of the votes in the local election held earlier this month, the African National Congress (ANC) has delivered its weakest ever electoral performance in over three decades of South Africa’s post-apartheid era. Held amid worsening water shortages, power disruptions, and piling uncollected garbage, the party saw its vote share drop by almost 15 percentage points from the 45.6% it received in the 2021 local elections. The number of council seats it secured dropped over 30%, from 4,548 in 2021 to 3,164 in 2026.​ Even steeper is the more than 68% decline in the number of municipalities where it has an outright majority. In the 2021 local election, the ANC won outright majorities in 161 of the 213 municipalities. In this election, only 51. Its loss is particularly severe in urban areas. In 2021, the ANC was the largest party in six of the eight metropolitan municipalities. In two of them, it secured an outright majority with over 50% of the seats. In the 2026 local election, however, it failed to secure an outright majority in any municipality. It retained a simple majority status in only two – Buffalo City and Mangaung. Center-right DA’s gains are mainly in urban areas The center-right Democratic Alliance (DA), which in 2021 had already won the highest number of votes in Nelson Mandela Bay and an outright majority of seats in Cape Town, went on to replace the ANC as the largest party in Johannesburg, Tshwane, and Ekurhuleni. It retained the outright majority in Cape Town. In the remaining seven municipalities, no party has won an outright majority, even though the DA has the highest votes in five of the eight metropolitan municipalities. Beyond its metropolitan gains, however, the DA has captured only a fraction of ANC’s loss. Its vote share increased by barely 3 percentage points, from 21.66% in 2021 to 24.6% in 2026. Its total council seats increased from 1,496 to 1,527. Historically associated with the interests of the wealthy white minority, the DA emerged as the principal electoral challenger to the ANC. Winning South Africa’s first democratic election after leading the anti-apartheid struggle, the ANC came to power in 1994, with Nelson Mandela as president. It ruled for 30 years without needing any coalitions, outside of the tripartite alliance, winning an outright majority of parliamentary seats in all subsequent national elections until 2024, when it fell short of the minimum 201 seats required to form a government, securing only 159 of the 400. From its peak vote share of 69.69% in the 2004 national election, the ANC has consistently lost support in every successive election, dropping to just over 40% of the vote in 2024. Adopting neoliberal policies, the ANC failed to correct the economic injustices of the apartheid regime. Under rampant privatization, the public sector suffered. Unemployment soared, especially among Black Africans. People’s movements like Abahlali baseMjondolo, fighting for land rights of the urban poor, faced severe repression. Read more: “A declaration of war against the poor”: AbM leads resistance against South Africa’s anti-occupation bill When ANC joined hands with the right Instead of correcting its course, the ANC joined hands with the DA – which had been advocating an even more aggressive pursuit of neoliberal policies – to form the Government of National Unity (GNU), along with eight other smaller parties , including ethno-nationalist and far-right parties. Two years later, in the 2026 local election, the ANC was dealt another severe blow with less than 31% of the vote, its lowest countrywide share in any election before – national, provincial or local. “This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC,” said the party’s secretary general, Fikile Mbalula. “We cannot ask the people to trust us merely because of our history.”​ The DA, on the other hand, gained one million black voters, said its leader, Geordin Hill-Lewis, who is also the mayor of Cape Town. However, it added up to only a small fraction of the 15% vote share the ANC lost. Most of it was gained by smaller opposition parties opposed to the GNU.​ Led by former ANC chief and the ex-President of South Africa, Jacob Zuma, the uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP) won 9.61% of the vote in its first local election. Taking the name of the ANC’s armed wing during the anti-Apartheid struggle, it splintered from the ANC in late 2023. It secured 14.58% of the vote in the 2024 national election, supplanting the Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) as the third-largest party in Parliament. Its manifesto called for nationalization of several sectors, reversal of privatization, and a greater state role in the economy. However, critics have questioned its credibility, pointing to the contradiction between its manifesto and the record of its leader, Jacob Zuma, who presided over the implementation of neoliberal economic policies during his presidency from 2009 to 2018.​ Xenophobic, far-right parties in ascent Earlier this year, ahead of the local elections, the MKP, which many describe as a far-right party , was linked to xenophobic mobilizations targeting poor immigrants from other African countries. Winning 701 council seats and outright majorities in five municipalities, and emerging as the largest party in 19, the MKP replaced the EFF as the third-largest party at the municipal level The left-populist EFF is itself a splinter of the ANC, formed in 2013 by its former Youth League president, Julius Malema, after he was expelled from the party. It received 6.25% of the vote in 2026, down from over 10% in the 2021 local elections. Finishing close on the heels of the EFF is the ascendant ActionSA, which secured 5.67% of the vote, more than doubling the 2.33% it had in 2021. A breakaway from the DA, ActionSA is also a far-right party, advocating xenophobic anti-immigrant measures. However, unlike the MKP, whose xenophobia is combined with state-interventionist economic proposals, ActionSA combines its xenophobia with free-market fundamentalism. Winning the sixth-highest vote share, close behind ActionSA with 4.69% of the vote, is the Zulu ethno-nationalist Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP), which prides itself on its anti-socialist identity and advocates social conservatism and a free market. Its vote share dropped only slightly from 5.64% in 2021. It is a part of the GNU, along with the ANC and the DA.​ Also part of the GNU is the Freedom Front Plus (FFP), which secured the seventh-highest number of votes, slightly increasing its share from 2.34% in 2021 to 2.99% in 2026. It is a far-right Afrikaner White nationalist party rooted in the apartheid era elite. Communist Party’s electoral debut Trailing just behind with the eighth-highest number of votes is the South African Communist Party (SACP), which secured 2.38% in the very first election it has contested independently. Although the party is more than 100 years old and was on the frontlines of the anti-apartheid struggle, it aligned itself with the ANC since the democratic breakthrough in 1994, and had never before contested independently in any election. However, in 2024, after the ANC joined hands with the center-right DA to form the GNU, which even included the far-right Afrikaner FFP, the SACP decided to contest the 2026 local election independently, without breaking the historic tripartite alliance. It secured over 700,000 votes and 271 council seats, giving hope to the left in an election whose results otherwise point to an ascendant right. Unprecedented number of hung councils ​ Well over 500 more parties contested in this race, fielding about 137,000 candidates for 10,526 council seats, according to the Electoral Commission of South Africa. South Africa has 213 municipalities, but a revote is pending in one. Of the 212 municipalities with declared results, only 73 have a party holding more than 50% of council seats. The remaining 139 are hung councils, where no party has an outright majority. Despite massive losses, the ANC, which remains the single largest party, has opened talks with all parties.​ “This situation has imposed on all political parties a duty to reflect and determine the best and most stable coalitions” for these 139 municipalities, it said on November 15.

articles.title: People’s Climate March: Thousands Demonstrate in Turkey as Country Hosts COP31 U.N. Summit
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : We are broadcasting from the U.N. climate summit, COP31, here in Antalya, Turkey. More than 190 countries are attending the summit, but for the second year in a row, the United States has not sent an official delegation. Shortly after returning to the White House, President Trump withdrew the U.S. from the landmark 2015 Paris Climate Agreement. Here at COP31, climate activists have been demanding immediate action to confront the climate crisis. Earlier today, activists rallied against the plastics industry. PROTESTERS : Less plastics! More life! Less plastics! More life! Less plastics! More life! Less plastics! More life! Less plastics! More life! AMY GOODMAN : Over the weekend, Democracy Now! was in the streets of Antalya as thousands of protesters marched to demand urgent climate action. Democracy Now! ’s Anjali Kamat filed this report. PROTESTER : We are children of this planet! We have a right on this planet! ANJALI KAMAT : Over 10,000 people came out in the streets of Antalya, Turkey, this Saturday to participate in the People’s Climate March. PROTESTERS : The people, united, will never be defeated! ANJALI KAMAT : Despite a light rain, the mood was festive and defiant, with people from across Turkey and around the world demanding stronger climate action. From Indigenous rights to making polluters pay to ending the genocide in Gaza and the war in Iran, the protesters connected the dots. PROTESTERS : Free, free Palestine! Free, free Palestine! Worker power! Worker power! KIVANÇ ELIAÇIK: This is Kıvanç Eliaçık, labor activist. I’m with People’s Climate Summit. I’m based in Istanbul normally. Fossil fuels are killing the planet. Of course, there are a long list of demands, but from a trade union perspective, we are asking for a just transition, which we mean we want exit from fossil fuels, but we want job security, income security or pension rights. So we are asking for just transition. We want to keep the planet, but we want to keep the jobs, as well. ANJALI KAMAT : Just as the COP opened last week, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan announced the discovery of two new oil fields in the southeast of the country. Kıvanç is one of the organizers of an alternative People’s Climate Summit that kicked off with Saturday’s march. KIVANÇ ELIAÇIK: Turkey is co-hosting COP31 together with Australia. They are also destroying the nature to build new infrastructures to host this event. And while having the COP31 presidency, co-presidency here, Turkey has no plan for exit of fossil fuels. So, the meeting, the Turkish co-presidency focused on zero waste. It’s an important issue. Recycling, waste management is important issue. But we have no plans about fossil fuels. So we need a plan for fossil fuels. PROTESTERS : Workers, united, will never be defeated! ANJALI KAMAT : Labor groups made up a large portion of the march. Nearly 80 unions from over 40 countries met in Antalya last week to call for more public solutions to the climate crisis. PROTESTERS : Worker power! Worker power! Worker power! Worker power! LALA PEÑARANDA: My name is Lala Peñaranda. I’m the Latin America coordinator at Trade Unions for Energy Democracy. I’m based in Bogotá, Colombia. Trade unions care about a lot more than just protecting jobs. We have systemic demands. It’s really to reject the “privatize to decarbonize” agenda, to the fight for energy as a human right, not as a commodity. ANJALI KAMAT : When you say “privatize to decarbonize,” what do you mean by that? LALA PEÑARANDA: We saw a growing trend of both institutions, like the IMF and the World Bank, but also even some actors in the trade union movement, that were saying, “You know what? As long as we have a seat at the table, we’re fine. You can privatize energy, you can privatize public services, as long as we have a seat at the table and we have a job.” And we were saying, “No, no, the trade union tradition is to defend the working class — not the unions, not the union bureaucracy, the working class.” And that means that our public services, starting with energy, has to be public. It has to be in public hands, and it has to be for the people. AKHATOR JOEL ODIGIE : Akhator Joel Odigie is my name, general secretary of the African Regional Organisation of the International Trade Union Confederation. ANJALI KAMAT : And where are you coming from, sir? AKHATOR JOEL ODIGIE : I am coming from Lomé, Togo. That’s where I am headquartered. ANJALI KAMAT : And what is your main demand? AKHATOR JOEL ODIGIE : Just transition for workers that is inclusive, that is financed. And more than ever before, the Belém plan of action, we need to begin implementation now. And we are not seeing that, unfortunately. The planet is heating up. We cannot continue to pretend that things are the same. They are not the same. ANJALI KAMAT : And are people inside the COP31 meeting — are they addressing any of this? AKHATOR JOEL ODIGIE : This is a challenge, we are saying. They are not listening as we would want. There is so much slowdown. To get to all of these, we need huge financing. Polluters must pay. Those that are polluting the climate should come forward with the resources. SUNGHEE OH: OK, I’m SungHee Oh from South Korea, South Korean trade union. ANJALI KAMAT : Are you feeling hopeful about anything coming out of this formal summit? SUNGHEE OH: Not really, because, you know, the labor unions around the world, we have been demanding a just transition, you know, with guaranteed workers’ rights for many years. And they agreed to have a just transition mechanism in the COP30 — I mean, the COP governance, but they haven’t been able to include, you know, trade unions and workers in the negotiations. So, I don’t know. I’m not so sure. That’s why we gather here, and, you know, we try to put pressure on, you know, those government parties in the negotiation tables. PROTESTERS : Polluters have to pay! Polluters have to pay! What do we want? Climate justice! What do we want? Climate justice! ANJALI KAMAT : We also met a farmer from Pakistan who lost his harvest and livestock in the catastrophic floods of 2022 that displaced over 30 million people and inundated millions of acres of farmland. ABDUL KHALIQUE LAGHARI : [translated] My name is Abdul Khalique Laghari. I’m from Dadu Province in Sindh, Pakistan. ANJALI KAMAT : Laghari is part of a group of nearly 40 flood-affected farmers who are suing two of Germany’s most polluting companies for their emissions. They’re suing on the basis of a German court ruling last year that opened the door to companies being held liable for climate damages caused by their carbon emissions. Pakistan contributes less than 1% to global carbon emissions. Nasir Mansour from the National Trade Union Federation of Pakistan is supporting the lawsuit. NASIR MANSOUR : We have made the polluters accountable. So, we are not only asking for a compensation, but we are all asking for the justice. So, it’s a symbolic kind of our venture. It will give a new boost and the hope to the other communities who suffer from the climatic displacement and the calamities. ANJALI KAMAT : It wasn’t just groups from Turkey and the Global South at the march, but also activists from Europe still reeling from the heat waves this summer that killed over 50,000 people. SORAYA FETTIH : My name is Soraya Fettih. I work for 350.org. I’m based in the southwest of France. Just last summer, I saw part of my region just burned to the ground because, yet once again, our politicians are doing almost nothing to fight the climate crisis that is happening. We lost people. We lost, like, our fields, some of our means of, like, livelihood. So, for me, coming here was a way to protest, fight for what’s needed. ANJALI KAMAT : And, Soraya, are you going to be at the COP , or are you outside this whole week? SORAYA FETTIH : I’m doing both. Like, I feel like we have to be everywhere and give it our all, because, again, like, the climate emergency, we can all feel it wherever we are right now. It used to be mostly the countries and the populations from the so-called Global South, those who did the least to, like, create this crisis, that would feel the most impact. But right now we are all feeling it, whether you are from the North or the South. And so, the urgency that we’re feeling, we need to translate it in proper action and hire the pressure, again, on our leaders and on our governments right now. They are just, like, not doing enough. ANJALI KAMAT : As the march came to an end in Antalya’s Republic Square, the sun was out, and a group of Turkish activists unfurled rainbow flags and burst into song. *PROTESTERS: [singing] O bella ciao, bella ciao, bella ciao, ciao, ciao… ANJALI KAMAT : While climate justice was the focus of Saturday’s march, many of the participating Turkish groups raised concerns over domestic repression in other arenas. In September, Turkish authorities launched nationwide raids against the LGBTQ+ community, arresting over a hundred activists. YAĞMUR ORHAN : We hide the flags on our backs, and then we open them. So we were able to use them today. ANJALI KAMAT : This is Yağmur Orhan, a 21-year-old activist. YAĞMUR ORHAN : We are starting a campaign called We Want Freedom. And we demand that our friends will be released immediately and stop this madness, honestly. ANJALI KAMAT : Is there a sense of fear in the community, given the scale of the crackdown? YAĞMUR ORHAN : It’s honestly a very scary environment. We feel that in our communities, in our homes, in our everyday lives, because we are being arrested, we are being accused of nonsense crimes, so that we can feel that very much. But we are sticking together. We are fighting against this together. So, we’re going to be OK. I’m sure about that. ANJALI KAMAT : Do you feel like people are able to come out and say proudly that they are part of the LGBTQ community in Turkey? YAĞMUR ORHAN : No, I don’t really think that. Trans people cannot transition because of this environment. People are scared of their families, the people, the government. So, not a very safe space right now. ANJALI KAMAT : If people say, “How is this related to climate?” what would you say? YAĞMUR ORHAN : We know today that the fascist government that is attacking the LGBTQ people today is the same one that attacks the nature, the animals, the people. So, we know that this is an intersectionality problem, so we are here today. ANJALI KAMAT : As the gathering came to a close, we also ran into some veteran campaigners who have been advocating for climate justice for decades, both inside the COP and on the streets. ASAD REHMAN : My name is Asad Rehman. I’m from Friends of the Earth in England, Wales, Northern Ireland. We are in the midst of a crisis, of a crisis of crisis. We could see that with the killer floods, droughts and famines impacting people everywhere. Our ecosystems are collapsing. The U.N. has warned we’re about to breach the critical 1.5-degree guardrail with devastating consequences on all of that happening, of course, on top of a global inequality crisis, where the rich and powerful are getting richer and richer, and more and more people are struggling to survive. So, we come to these climate talks with an urgent need for, one, governments to — especially the rich countries to do their fair share of action and to provide much-needed resources and finance, particularly for those on the frontlines, not just in the Global South now, but increasingly in the Global North, as well. Will rich countries provide real public finance? Now, let me tell you, just five oil companies in the last nine months have made profits five times the amount that the rich countries have handed over in public climate finance. There is abundant wealth, but it’s obviously in the hands of a very, very few people. HARJEET SINGH : I’m Harjeet Singh. I’m with the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative and Fill the Fund campaign. We want finance in the form of grants. We don’t want money that is going to further exacerbate the debt crisis. Developing countries are already struggling. And the reality is that developed countries only want to see how they can make money from this process and not to help communities who are facing the climate crisis right now. Unless and until finance is provided by developed countries, nothing is going to move. That’s the reality. Or, if we don’t see action on phasing out fossil fuels, we are going to see this crisis only intensifying, and that’s what we are seeing. Look at how we have actually breached the 1.5 degree Celsius target, and disasters are everywhere, not just in developing countries. Even the developed world is suffering now. KUMI NAIDOO : My name is Kumi Naidoo. I’m from South Africa. I’m the president of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative. Today, the fossil fuel industry holds a roughly morally equivalent position of what the slave-owning class did. They occupy — because, you know, the slave owners, when we were — people were saying, “We need a phaseout. It’s inhumane, and it’s a violation of all our religions,” and so on, they would say, “Oh, if we stop doing slavery, the whole world will fall apart. Impossible!” All those arguments that they gave, you will hear it now from the fossil fuel industry. “Everything will fall down,” and so on. And let’s hope that the fossil fuel industry gets a message that their days are numbered. And, you know, people must just remember one thing: Nobody anticipated the Berlin Wall would come down as fast as it did. Everybody thought it was going to be forever. And it happened. I believe that the fall of the fossil fuel industry will happen in the same way. And this moment needs, calls for massive, peaceful civil disobedience against the fossil fuel companies wherever they are, wherever they continue to operate. And I’m seeing it happening, and I think it’s going to grow in leaps and bounds in the months to come. ANJALI KAMAT : For Democracy Now! , this is Anjali Kamat, with Hany Massoud and Nicole Salazar. AMY GOODMAN : And thanks so much to Anjali, Hany and Nicole for that report from the streets of Antalya, Turkey, for the People’s Climate March on the Global Day of Climate Action this past Saturday. Coming up, Farhana Yamin, a climate negotiator who’s been to nearly every COP — that’s climate summit — over the last 30 years. She helped negotiate the 1.5 degree Celsius limit in the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement, that is now on track to be surpassed. What does this mean? We’ll get her reaction, and we’ll also speak to Asad Rehman from Friends of the Earth. Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : Casey Camp-Horinek of the Ponca Nation of Oklahoma, here at the People’s Climate Summit taking place in Antalya on Sunday.

articles.title: Global Warming Approaches 1.5 Degrees in “Calamity for the World’s Ecosystems”
articles.content: As delegates, industry lobbyists and civil society activists attend this year’s United Nations climate summit, known as COP31, we speak with international environmental lawyer Farhana Yamin about the state of global climate efforts. Yamin helped write the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement and has attended 28 of the last 31 U.N. climate summits. The Paris Agreement aimed to keep global temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, a threshold that climate scientists say the world will now overshoot. “It’s a moment of great sadness, actually, for the world community that we weren’t able to start the phaseout, start the acceleration of the transition away from fossil fuels 10 years earlier,” says Yamin. “So, we’re about 10 years behind, but I hope that over time that we can accelerate.”

articles.title: “Coffers Are Never Empty…For Bombs”: Climate Activist Asad Rehman on Need for Climate Finance
articles.content: The United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, is in its second and final week. To get an update on the state of negotiations among countries, we speak with longtime climate campaigner Asad Rehman, the chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland. He says rich, developed countries are still dragging their feet on a rapid transition away from fossil fuels while withholding the money that poorer, Global South countries need. “Whether you’re cutting emissions, whether you’re adapting to the impacts of climate change or dealing with incredible losses which are totalling over a trillion right now, you need public finance,” says Rehman. “And the rich countries are saying, 'Our coffers are empty.' But, of course, the coffers are never empty when it comes to paying for bombs. It’s never empty when it comes to the fossil fuel subsidies to the corporate giants, and it’s never empty when it comes to the billionaires.”

articles.title: Israeli forces arrest groom at his wedding in attack on West Bank village
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: The Israeli forces escalated their assaults on the village of Al-Mughayyir in the central occupied West Bank between Wednesday, November 11 and Friday, November 13. On Wednesday, the Israeli military’s bulldozers and excavators razed lands belonging to Palestinian citizens from the village to construct a new settlement road. This came days after bulldozing olive orchards in Al-Mughayyir, which resulted in uprooting about 12,000 trees . One day later, Israeli forces destroyed the martyrs’ memorial in Al-Mughayyir. Meanwhile, on Friday, they raided the house of a Palestinian citizen, forcing him and his family to evacuate after blocking the only entrance to the village. Hours later, Israeli troops stormed a ballroom where a wedding was being held and arrested four Palestinians, including the groom, who was taken to an unknown location. According to local media outlets, roughly 150 invitees, including women, were held inside the ballroom, attacked with tear gas, and searched. Reports indicated that soldiers confiscated some women’s jewelry during the searches, while young men were briefly detained and beaten nearby. On the same evening, the Israeli military raided a school in the village and summoned its director to the scene immediately, with no further details reported about the incident. Al-Mughayyir is among several villages east of Ramallah that have increasingly faced Israeli settler violence, frequent military raids, land bulldozing, and restrictions on movement. These assaults have increased in 2026. Read more: Settler violence escalates in the West Bank. Understand why it is concentrated east of Ramallah At least six Palestinians, including four children and one teenager, have been killed at the hands of illegal Israeli settlers and Israeli forces since the beginning of the year. The fatalities were: Mohammed Na’saan (14) Aws Na’saan (14) Khalil Abu Alia (16) Fadi Na’saan (17) Omar Na’san (19) Jihad Abu Naim (30s) Read more: As Israeli violence escalates, Palestinian youth increasingly identify as ‘martyrs-to-be’

articles.title: Former Bolivian VP granted political asylum by Mexico
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: Former Bolivian vice president Álvaro García Linera is currently in Mexico where he has been granted political asylum. Shortly after, the Bolivian Attorney General’s Office requested Interpol issue a Blue Notice to locate García Linera for alleged crimes of murder and torture. This was reported by Police Commander Adrián Álvarez. For his part, presidential spokesperson José Luis Gálvez said that García Linera had left the country, first to Argentina and then to Mexico. García Linera himself reported on Friday that Mexico has granted his request for political asylum: “I am in Mexico and I have political asylum in Mexico.” This is not the first time Mexico has granted this status to the former vice president. Back in 2019, following the coup against Morales, both top leaders of the MAS arrived in Mexico from Bolivia under asylum status. According to the state prosecutors , Evo Morales (the country’s former president from 2006 to 2019) and García Linera were responsible for the police raid on a hotel in Santa Cruz in 2009, in which three people were killed. Meanwhile, the government at the time said that the police succeeded in dismantling a terrorist and separatist cell. The three people killed were accused of being part of a cell that sought to carry out terrorist operations to promote the secession of the Santa Cruz region from Bolivia. An arrest warrant has been outstanding against Evo Morales for several months for other alleged crimes, but the former president has decided to remain in Bolivia, surrounded by his supporters, and has not yet been apprehended by the police. Morales has denounced the charges against him as a clear act of political persecution against the leaders of the progressive MAS (Movement Toward Socialism) government, which succeeded in establishing the first government led by an Indigenous person in the history of Bolivia – one of the countries with the highest concentration of Indigenous people in the world. Regarding the charges in the case involving García Linera, Morales said : “I’m not going to leave [the country]; I’m going to face the music; I’m going to defend myself; we’re going to defend the unity of the national territory against those who want to divide it – that’s why they’re prosecuting me.” Unlike Morales, who has maintained a clearly influential public profile in Bolivia’s political landscape, García Linera has devoted himself primarily to academic activities, though he has always expressed his political views on current events. García Linera is widely recognized as one of the most important critical and intellectual voices not only in Bolivia but throughout Latin America. The Supreme Court of Justice has warned that if García Linera does not appear in court, he will be declared “in contempt,” which would justify his arrest. And based on the sequence of events, it appears that this will indeed be the prosecution’s decision. For its part, the Bolivian Ministry of Foreign Affairs has requested an explanation from Mexico regarding the as-yet-unconfirmed political asylum granted to García Linera, and warned that the possible decision will not halt the judicial investigations into a case that many claim is more about political persecution than anything else, although the Bolivian government asserts that it is a process aimed at seeking justice. Nadia Beller , Bolivian attorney and ex-girlfriend of right-wing political operative Fernando Cerimedo also requested and was granted political asylum in Mexico. Read more: Ex-partner of powerful far-right Latin American political operator receives asylum in Mexico

articles.title: ‘Monster data centers’ being built in Scotland for US tech companies met with protests
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: Thousands of people took to the streets of Edinburgh on Saturday, November 14, to protest against the massive expansion of data centers in Scotland. “Developers want to build monster data centers across Scotland and sell them on to big US tech companies,” the Stop AI Data Centers Scotland coalition wrote in the protest announcement. “There are over 20 already proposed and more in the pipeline, which would demand twice as much electricity as Scotland’s peak usage. This has huge consequences for our energy bills, water, health, communities, climate and nature.” Dozens of organizations that joined the coalition and protest – including climate justice associations, anti-war groups, and trade unions – have demanded accountability from the Scottish government: a pause on expansion plans, proper impact studies, and public consultations. “Decisions on AI data centers should be led by the people, not by big tech profits,” they said. “The people of Scotland must have a say on how our public resources are used.” Data centers return nothing to host communities Environmental organizations are warning that Scotland is becoming an increasingly attractive location for data centers due to “cheap land and cool climate.” But the Scottish government’s continuous referencing of “green data centers” – a term yet to be fully defined – as a development pathway cannot be dismissed as additional encouragement. This goes hand in hand with promises of data centers bringing more jobs, despite calculations showing these would number in the hundreds at best. Read more: Meta wants to build a $50 billion data center in Louisiana As a result, workers in Scotland would effectively bear the brunt of the massive data centers through increased costs of living and environmental devastation. “They demand massive public infrastructure and resource support,” emphasized Claire Robertson of the Edinburgh Trade Union Council, “yet return virtually no secure, permanent, or unionized jobs for the local communities forced to host them.” Environmental and health concerns The scale of many proposed data centers is a particular concern for the public. Action to Protect Rural Scotland (APRS) warned that planned hyper-scale data centers are one hundred times bigger than existing data centers. “The 1000 MW site proposed in Chapelcross, Annan would require the energy equivalent of a quarter of the entire peak demand of Scotland,” APRS found. “It would take Whitelees Windfarm, the largest onshore wind farm in the UK, eight years to generate the energy to power this site for just one year.” Read more: A massive AI data center transforms rural Utah into a national flashpoint Adding to fears about the impact on public infrastructure and the cost of living, health groups joined the mobilizations, emphasizing that data centers represent health hazards as well. The People’s Health Movement (PHM) Scotland is among the networks joining the protest, insisting that the mushrooming of data centers brings risks for heart and respiratory health through air pollution, the risk of skin diseases “arising from contaminated water entering the water supply,” and hearing loss and tinnitus as a consequence of noise pollution. PHM Scotland also highlighted the possibility of “increased mental health problems arising from loss of green space, noise pollution and the additional localized heat burden created by large data centers.” Ties to the military-industrial complex In addition to fears about consequences for local communities, organizations endorsing the protest expressed concerns about the potential international impact of hyper-scale data centers. “The rise of AI and the growing power of the tech oligarchy are intimately tied to the military-industrial complex,” said Coll McCail of Stop the War Scotland. “The Pentagon, for example, has already adopted an ‘AI first’ approach to warfare, spending 9 billion USD on data centers.” Protesters called for a pause on existing development plans, proper impact studies, and public consultations. Source: Climate Camp Scotland/Facebook “Closer to home, Peter Thiel’s Palantir has embedded itself within the Ministry of Defense, and the UK government has contracted Raytheon to train 60,000 soldiers in military AI every year. Scotland’s proposed data centers may yet be put in service for such aims, without sufficient public debate or discussion.” People’s Health Dispatch is a monthly bulletin published by the People’s Health Movement and Peoples Dispatch . articles.title: Iran warns there will be no geographical limit to its retaliation
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: In the latest round of “tit-for-tat” attacks, Iran claimed it destroyed the US army’s early warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday, November 13, in retaliation to its attack against its telecommunication tower in Sirik earlier. In the statement , the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) also reiterated the warning to the “aggressor enemy to cease its aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz” and other countries aiding in its aggression. Meanwhile, the Iranian Navy claimed at least two more oil tankers caught fire after they violated its warnings and tried to enter the prohibited area of the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday. The tankers had switched off their radar system and entered the “unsafe” area when they hit sea mines and caught fire, it claimed. In recent weeks, scores of tankers and ships have been hit in a similar manner while trying to cross the Strait of Hormuz, bypassing Iranian restrictions. On Wednesday, two super tankers reportedly carrying over 4 million barrels of oil had suffered similar explosions after failing to comply with Iranian warnings. The regular attacks on oil tankers contradicts US claims of control over the Strait of Hormuz and the normalization of oil shipments in the waterway through which nearly a quarter of global energy trade passes. Iran’s retaliation will have no geographical boundary On Thursday, Mohsen Rezaei, chief of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) had warned the US that if it “launches another war against Iran, every military base involved in the aggression – from West Asia to Europe – will be a legitimate target for Iran’s lethal strikes.” “No safe distance. No safe heaven. No immunity,” he said in a post on X. During an interview with Al-Mayadeen earlier he explained that unlike in the previous rounds, the Iranian retaliation to any fresh US attack will have no geographical limitation. He claimed the decision about this has been made on the basis of orders issued by Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei last month. Iran has already removed the 2,000 mile restrictions on its missile ranges, various Iranian military officials have been reported saying by the Iranian media in recent days. In the previous rounds of the war, Iranian retaliation against US military bases and assets were limited to the region. US President Donald Trump has given mixed signals about the war on Iran. In his recent statements, he has admitted there was no further need of restarting the war without ruling out limited targeted attacks on its nuclear facilities. Reacting to a statement issued after the G7 Foreign Ministers meeting on Thursday about their possible involvement in US efforts in the Strait of Hormuz, Esmail Baghaei, official spokesperson of Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, warned all foreign governments against providing any kind of military or logistical support to the US even on the pretext of protecting “freedom of navigation.” Any such assistance would be considered an “unlawful act of aggression” against Iran and would invite Iranian retaliation, Baghaei warned. The ball is in Washington’s court In an interview with Al-Jazeera on Wednesday, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, speaker of Iran’s Parliament and its chief negotiator, claimed that Iran has conveyed a clear and reasonable response to the US setting out its conditions and now the US has to decide how it would like to take it forward. “Iran would like to end the no war no peace situation,” he said claiming “we are not warmongers, we are not seeking war, and we do not want war to continue.” Ghalibaf also dismissed the claims made by Secretary of State Marco Rubio that the Iranian conditions were unreasonable. How are the lifting of the blockade, removing sanctions, and ending the war on all fronts “unreasonable,” Ghalibaf asked, claiming that these are the basic minimum demands concerning the Iranian people and the US must accept them if it wants further engagement. Underlining the lack of trust with the US; it has attacked Iran during the ongoing negotiations twice and has violated the June 17 Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), weeks after signing it, Ghalibaf argued that it is natural that Iran is very cautious about any future deal. Ghalibaf reiterated the Iranian position that the presence of the US military in the region has created insecurity rather than stability and the countries in the region must work together to establish lasting security without outside interference. During his meeting with the representatives of Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan earlier this month, Rezaei had reportedly proposed the formation of an eight-country Gulf Union, including the six Gulf countries and Iran and Iraq. The three countries have recently formed a collective security group called the Mecca Defense Pact and are seeking to increase its membership.
